nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin B12 is exclusively absorbed in the terminal ileum via intrinsic factor receptors. Crohn's disease most commonly affects the terminal ileum, and chronic inflammation damages the specialized absorptive cells (enterocytes) responsible for B12 uptake. Even without surgery, active ileal disease can cause severe B12 malabsorption. Deficiency develops insidiously because the liver stores 2-5 years' worth of B12.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Surgical removal of the terminal ileum eliminates the only site in the body capable of active B12 absorption. Resections of more than 60 cm of terminal ileum virtually guarantee permanent B12 malabsorption requiring lifelong supplementation. Even resections of 20-60 cm significantly impair absorption. Passive diffusion accounts for only about 1% of oral B12 absorption, making oral supplementation unreliable after ileal resection.
deficiency_symptoms: Megaloblastic anemia (large, immature red blood cells)
Numbness and tingling in hands and feet (peripheral neuropathy)
Cognitive changes: memory loss, confusion, difficulty concentrating
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (severe, irreversible)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 22-33% of Crohn's patients overall; up to 48% in patients with ileal disease or prior ileal resection

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 100-500 mcg/day oral or 1000 mcg/month intramuscular, depending on disease location
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 1000 mcg intramuscular every 1-3 months (lifelong if >60 cm ileum resected); high-dose oral (1000-2000 mcg/day) may work for minor resections via passive diffusion

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Methylcobalamin or hydroxocobalamin (intramuscular injection for post-resection patients)
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Methylcobalamin is the bioactive coenzyme form, requiring no conversion. Hydroxocobalamin has longer tissue retention than cyanocobalamin. After ileal resection, intramuscular injection bypasses the destroyed absorption site entirely.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Cyanocobalamin is acceptable but less efficient; requires conversion and releases trace cyanide. Sublingual forms are unreliable after ileal resection.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 1000 mcg/day oral (methylcobalamin) or 1000 mcg IM monthly
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 1000 mcg IM injection every 1-3 months (standard); some protocols use 1000 mcg IM weekly for 4 weeks to replete, then monthly. High-dose oral (2000 mcg/day) may suffice for minor resections (<20 cm) via passive diffusion (~1% absorbed).
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Injections are the gold standard after ileal resection. If using oral supplements, take on an empty stomach for best passive absorption. Sublingual may offer slight advantage over swallowed tablets. Avoid taking with high-dose vitamin C (>500 mg) which may degrade B12.
interactions: Metformin reduces B12 absorption by 10-30%
Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2 blockers reduce B12 release from food
Colchicine impairs B12 absorption
Nitrous oxide inactivates B12 stores (relevant for anesthesia)
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Resection of >60 cm of terminal ileum, active severe ileal disease, documented malabsorption despite high-dose oral therapy, or serum B12 remains low after 3 months of oral supplementation.

lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months; also check methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine as functional markers when B12 is borderline (200-400 pg/mL)
lab_monitoring.notes: Serum B12 alone can be misleading. MMA >0.4 umol/L and homocysteine >15 umol/L suggest functional deficiency even with normal serum B12. Holotranscobalamin (active B12) is a more sensitive early marker if available.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Both B12 and folate metabolism are affected; methotrexate is a folate antagonist but B12 status should be adequate for proper folate cycling
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor B12 and folate together; supplement both as needed

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Impairs folate absorption; may mask B12 deficiency if folate is supplemented without checking B12
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Always check B12 before starting folate supplementation

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Reduce gastric acid needed to release B12 from food proteins
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Use supplemental B12 (not food-bound) or injections

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Indirectly related; adequate B12 and folate needed for proper DNA synthesis and to avoid compounding myelosuppression
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Ensure B12 is replete before and during therapy

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin requiring bile salts and intact intestinal mucosa for absorption. Crohn's disease causes fat malabsorption through mucosal damage, bile salt depletion (especially with ileal disease), and reduced dietary intake during flares. Vitamin D also plays an immunomodulatory role—deficiency is associated with increased Crohn's flare risk, higher disease activity, and greater need for surgery. It helps maintain intestinal barrier integrity.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Ileal resection disrupts bile salt reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation), leading to bile salt deficiency and fat malabsorption, which directly impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption including vitamin D. Extensive small bowel resection reduces the absorptive surface area. Post-resection patients also tend to avoid fatty foods (which are the primary dietary sources of vitamin D) due to steatorrhea.
deficiency_symptoms: Frequent infections due to impaired immunity
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 35-75% of Crohn's patients; prevalence increases with ileal disease, resection history, and northern latitudes

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 2000-5000 IU/day or higher with monitoring; some patients require 50,000 IU weekly for repletion. Dose guided by serum levels.

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) in oil-based softgel or liquid drops
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: D3 (cholecalciferol) raises and maintains serum 25(OH)D levels more effectively than D2 (ergocalciferol). Oil-based delivery improves absorption of this fat-soluble vitamin, especially critical in patients with fat malabsorption.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Dry tablet forms are poorly absorbed in fat malabsorption states. D2 (ergocalciferol) is less potent and shorter-acting than D3, though 50,000 IU D2 capsules remain useful for repletion protocols.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 1000-2000 IU/day maintenance; 50,000 IU weekly for 8-12 weeks for repletion
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 2000-5000 IU/day maintenance; repletion may require 50,000 IU 2-3 times per week for 8-12 weeks. Some patients with extensive resection need 10,000 IU/day. Always dose to serum level.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with the largest meal of the day containing some fat (even a small amount helps). Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil can improve absorption in fat-malabsorption states. Water-miscible (micellized) vitamin D preparations are available for severe malabsorption. Sunlight exposure (10-15 min midday) provides supplementary D3 synthesis but is unreliable.
interactions: Cholestyramine (bile acid sequestrant) significantly reduces vitamin D absorption—separate by 4+ hours
Corticosteroids impair calcium absorption and increase vitamin D catabolism
Orlistat reduces fat-soluble vitamin absorption
Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital increase vitamin D catabolism
Thiazide diuretics combined with vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe fat malabsorption with steatorrhea despite water-miscible preparations, serum 25(OH)D remains <20 ng/mL after 3 months of high-dose oral therapy, or short bowel syndrome. Intramuscular vitamin D (300,000 IU stoss therapy) or UV light therapy may be considered.

lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Every 3 months until stable in target range
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6 months; more frequently during dose adjustments or seasonal changes
lab_monitoring.notes: Target 30-50 ng/mL for Crohn's patients based on immunomodulatory benefit data. Check calcium and PTH simultaneously. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not useful for screening (tightly regulated, often normal even in deficiency). Recheck 3 months after dose changes.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Accelerate vitamin D catabolism and impair intestinal calcium absorption; increase osteoporosis risk
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Supplement vitamin D 2000-4000 IU/day and calcium during steroid use; obtain baseline DEXA scan if prolonged steroid course expected

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Binds bile salts and fat-soluble vitamins in the gut lumen
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Take vitamin D at least 4 hours before or after cholestyramine

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Some evidence that adequate vitamin D enhances biologic response; deficiency may reduce efficacy
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Optimize vitamin D levels before and during biologic therapy

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: No direct interaction, but these increase skin cancer risk; less sun exposure means less vitamin D synthesis
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Supplement vitamin D to compensate for necessary sun avoidance

Tetany or severe muscle spasms (suggests concurrent calcium deficiency)
Serum 25(OH)D <10 ng/mL with elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for immune function, gut epithelial integrity, and mucosal healing. Crohn's patients have impaired fat absorption, reduced dietary intake (avoidance of fruits and vegetables during flares), and increased utilization during active inflammation. Vitamin A deficiency impairs intestinal barrier function and mucosal repair, creating a cycle of worsening disease.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Ileal resection disrupts bile salt recycling, causing fat malabsorption and consequently poor absorption of all fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin A. Reduced small bowel surface area further limits absorption. Patients with extensive resection and steatorrhea are at highest risk.
deficiency_symptoms: Impaired mucosal regeneration in the gut
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 16-35% of Crohn's patients; higher in those with active disease, ileal involvement, or history of resection

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 900-1500 mcg RAE/day; monitor levels and adjust
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 1500-3000 mcg RAE/day with monitoring; water-miscible forms for severe malabsorption

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Retinyl palmitate (preformed vitamin A) in water-miscible or micellized form for malabsorption patients; beta-carotene as a safer alternative for maintenance
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Preformed vitamin A (retinyl palmitate) does not require conversion and is more reliably absorbed. Water-miscible preparations bypass the need for bile salt-dependent absorption. Beta-carotene is safer (no toxicity risk) but conversion to retinol is variable and less efficient.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: High-dose preformed vitamin A (>10,000 IU/day) without medical supervision due to hepatotoxicity risk. Avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic above 10,000 IU/day).
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 5000-10,000 IU/day (1500-3000 mcg RAE) for deficiency repletion; 2500-5000 IU/day maintenance
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 5000-10,000 IU/day with serum monitoring every 3-6 months; water-miscible form preferred. Adjust based on serum retinol levels.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with a meal containing fat. MCT oil can improve absorption. Water-miscible (ADEK) preparations are designed for fat malabsorption. Zinc is required for retinol-binding protein synthesis—ensure zinc is also adequate.
interactions: Cholestyramine reduces vitamin A absorption—separate by 4+ hours
Orlistat reduces fat-soluble vitamin absorption
Retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin) combined with vitamin A supplements risk hypervitaminosis A
Excessive alcohol intake increases hepatotoxicity risk of vitamin A
Warfarin: high-dose vitamin A may potentiate anticoagulant effect
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe steatorrhea unresponsive to water-miscible forms, short bowel syndrome with very limited absorptive capacity. Intramuscular vitamin A (100,000 IU) can be used for acute repletion under medical supervision.

lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Annually; more frequently if on high-dose supplementation to avoid toxicity
lab_monitoring.notes: Serum retinol is maintained by liver stores and only drops when stores are severely depleted—a low level indicates significant deficiency. Retinol-binding protein (RBP) is affected by inflammation and protein status. Check CRP simultaneously to interpret levels in context of inflammation.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage. Crohn's patients have increased oxidative stress from chronic inflammation and reduced antioxidant capacity. Fat malabsorption impairs vitamin E uptake, and dietary restrictions further limit intake.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Ileal resection causes bile salt deficiency and fat malabsorption, reducing vitamin E absorption. Vitamin E requires bile salts for micelle formation and absorption in the small intestine. Extensive resection shortens transit time and reduces absorptive surface.
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 10-20% of Crohn's patients; less commonly measured but likely underdiagnosed

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 30-60 mg/day with monitoring; water-miscible form for severe malabsorption

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: d-alpha-tocopherol (natural form) in water-miscible or micellized preparation
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Natural d-alpha-tocopherol has approximately twice the bioactivity of synthetic dl-alpha-tocopherol. Water-miscible forms bypass bile salt-dependent absorption.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: dl-alpha-tocopherol (synthetic—less bioactive). High-dose vitamin E (>400 IU/day) may increase all-cause mortality and bleeding risk.
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 400-800 IU/day water-miscible form during repletion; 200-400 IU/day maintenance. Monitor serum levels.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with a fat-containing meal. Water-miscible (ADEK) combination supplements are efficient for fat malabsorption. Vitamin C enhances vitamin E regeneration. Avoid simultaneous high-dose iron (competes for absorption).
interactions: Anticoagulants (warfarin): vitamin E may increase bleeding risk at doses >400 IU/day
Cholestyramine reduces vitamin E absorption
Orlistat reduces fat-soluble vitamin absorption
High-dose vitamin E may impair vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
Statins: some evidence of reduced antioxidant effect, clinical significance unclear
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe steatorrhea unresponsive to water-miscible preparations, short bowel syndrome. Intramuscular vitamin E is available but rarely needed.

lab_monitoring.notes: Serum vitamin E should be interpreted in relation to total lipids (alpha-tocopherol:lipid ratio) because levels are affected by lipid status. Ratio of <0.8 mg/g total lipids indicates deficiency even if absolute level appears normal.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting (coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X) and bone metabolism (osteocalcin activation). Crohn's patients are at risk due to fat malabsorption, dietary restrictions limiting green vegetable intake, antibiotic use disrupting gut bacteria that synthesize vitamin K2, and reduced bile salt availability.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Ileal resection causes bile salt depletion and fat malabsorption, impairing vitamin K1 absorption. Colonic resection eliminates a major site of vitamin K2 production by colonic bacteria. Antibiotic courses (common post-surgery) further deplete K2-producing gut flora.
deficiency_symptoms: Prolonged bleeding from cuts or wounds
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 20-50% have subclinical deficiency based on undercarboxylated osteocalcin or PIVKA-II; overt deficiency less common (~5-10%)

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 120-250 mcg/day; combination of K1 and K2
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 250-500 mcg/day or higher; monitor coagulation parameters

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Vitamin K2 as MK-7 (menaquinone-7) for bone health; K1 (phylloquinone) for coagulation support; combination supplements available
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: MK-7 has the longest half-life (72 hours vs 1-2 hours for K1), providing sustained levels. K1 is most important for coagulation. A combination of K1 + K2 (MK-7) covers both bone and coagulation needs.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Menadione (synthetic vitamin K3) is no longer recommended due to toxicity concerns.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 100-200 mcg K2 (MK-7)/day + 500 mcg K1/day for deficiency
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 200-500 mcg K2 (MK-7)/day; K1 5-10 mg/day if coagulopathy present. Water-miscible form preferred.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with a fat-containing meal (fat-soluble). Combination ADEK water-miscible supplements address all fat-soluble vitamins simultaneously. Vitamin D enhances vitamin K's bone benefits. Probiotics may help restore K2-producing gut flora.
interactions: Warfarin: vitamin K DIRECTLY ANTAGONIZES warfarin—dose must be consistent; consult anticoagulation clinic before supplementing
Antibiotics (especially broad-spectrum) deplete vitamin K2-producing gut bacteria
Cholestyramine reduces vitamin K absorption
Orlistat reduces fat-soluble vitamin absorption
High-dose vitamin A or E may interfere with vitamin K absorption
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Active bleeding with elevated INR requires IV vitamin K (phytonadione 10 mg slow IV). Severe malabsorption may require intramuscular K1 (10 mg weekly).

lab_monitoring.test_name: Prothrombin Time (PT) / INR; also Undercarboxylated Osteocalcin (ucOC) or PIVKA-II for subclinical deficiency
lab_monitoring.normal_range: PT: 11-13.5 seconds; INR: 0.8-1.1; ucOC not widely standardized
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: PT >14 seconds or INR >1.2 without anticoagulation
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Every 3 months; PT/INR with routine labs
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months; more frequently if on anticoagulants
lab_monitoring.notes: PT/INR only detects overt deficiency (coagulation affected). Undercarboxylated osteocalcin (ucOC) and PIVKA-II (proteins induced by vitamin K absence) are more sensitive markers of subclinical deficiency but not widely available. Serum phylloquinone can be measured but is affected by recent intake.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Co-supplement vitamin K2 with vitamin D and calcium during steroid use

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Iron deficiency is the single most common nutritional deficiency in Crohn's disease. It results from chronic intestinal blood loss (even microscopic), impaired duodenal/jejunal absorption due to inflammation, reduced dietary intake (meat avoidance, appetite loss), and hepcidin upregulation during inflammation that blocks iron absorption and mobilization from stores. Iron deficiency anemia significantly impacts quality of life.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. While these segments are less commonly resected, ileocecal resection can cause secondary duodenal inflammation or bacterial overgrowth affecting iron absorption. Anastomotic ulceration at the surgical site is a common source of chronic blood loss. Reduced transit time post-resection limits absorption time.
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 36-76% of Crohn's patients; iron deficiency anemia present in 30-50%

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: Guided by ferritin and hemoglobin; oral iron 50-200 mg elemental iron/day or IV iron if oral intolerant
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: IV iron preferred post-resection due to poor oral absorption and GI side effects; dose calculated by Ganzoni formula based on hemoglobin deficit

Non-heme iron; generally well-tolerated; pair with vitamin C source for better absorption

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose or iron sucrose) for active Crohn's or post-resection. Oral: ferrous bisglycinate (chelated iron) if oral route used.
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: IV iron bypasses the inflamed GI tract entirely, achieves faster repletion, and avoids GI side effects. Ferric carboxymaltose allows high single-dose infusions (up to 1000 mg). Oral ferrous bisglycinate (chelated) causes fewer GI side effects than ferrous sulfate and is better tolerated in IBD patients.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Ferrous sulfate causes significant GI side effects (nausea, constipation, diarrhea, cramping) and can worsen Crohn's inflammation by increasing oxidative stress in the gut lumen. Ferrous fumarate has similar issues. Avoid polysaccharide iron complex (poor absorption).
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: Oral: 50-100 mg elemental iron every other day (emerging evidence that alternate-day dosing improves fractional absorption). IV: dose calculated by Ganzoni formula.
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: IV iron strongly preferred: Ferric carboxymaltose 500-1000 mg IV over 15 min, repeat as needed based on calculation. If oral: ferrous bisglycinate 25-50 mg elemental iron every other day.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Oral iron absorbed best on empty stomach with vitamin C (250 mg). Take 2 hours apart from calcium, antacids, PPIs, dairy, coffee, and tea. Every-other-day dosing may be superior to daily (hepcidin rebound effect). Avoid concurrent zinc supplement (separate by 2 hours). IV iron has no food interactions.
interactions: PPIs and H2 blockers reduce gastric acid needed for iron solubility and absorption
Calcium supplements reduce iron absorption by 50-60% if taken together
Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics chelate iron—separate by 2+ hours
Zinc competes with iron for absorption—separate by 2 hours
Levothyroxine absorption reduced by iron—separate by 4 hours
Antacids (aluminum, magnesium) reduce iron absorption
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Hemoglobin <10 g/dL, ferritin <30 ng/mL with active inflammation, intolerance to oral iron, inadequate response after 4 weeks oral therapy, need for rapid repletion (pre-surgery), or concurrent erythropoietin therapy. ECCO/ESPEN guidelines recommend IV iron as first-line for active IBD.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Complete panel: Ferritin, Serum Iron, TIBC, Transferrin Saturation (TSAT), CBC with reticulocyte count, CRP
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Ferritin: 30-300 ng/mL (general) but >100 ng/mL target in active IBD due to inflammation; TSAT: 20-50%; Hemoglobin: 12-16 g/dL (women), 13.5-17.5 g/dL (men)
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: Ferritin <30 ng/mL in remission or <100 ng/mL with active inflammation (CRP elevated); TSAT <20%
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months in remission; every 3 months during active disease. ECCO recommends at minimum annually for all IBD patients.
lab_monitoring.notes: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant—elevated during inflammation even with iron deficiency. Always check CRP simultaneously. In active inflammation, ferritin <100 ng/mL suggests iron deficiency. TSAT <20% is a reliable marker regardless of inflammation. Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) is not affected by inflammation and can help distinguish iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Use IV iron or take oral iron with vitamin C; consider H2 blocker instead of PPI if possible

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May impair folate-dependent red blood cell production, compounding anemia
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor both iron and folate; supplement both as needed

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Folate antagonist; can compound anemia from iron deficiency
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Ensure adequate iron and folate; prescribed folate supplementation standard with methotrexate

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Recheck iron studies 3-6 months after starting biologic; oral iron may become effective

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Can mask anemia symptoms through mood/energy effects; may cause GI bleeding with long-term use
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor CBC regularly during steroid tapers

Chest pain or severe shortness of breath with anemia
Rapid heart rate (>120 bpm) at rest
Signs of GI bleeding: melena (black tarry stool), hematochezia (bright red blood), or significant drop in hemoglobin
Dizziness or syncope (fainting)

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Calcium deficiency in Crohn's is multifactorial: lactose intolerance leads to dairy avoidance (most common dietary calcium source), vitamin D deficiency impairs calcium absorption, corticosteroid use increases urinary calcium loss and reduces intestinal absorption, and chronic inflammation itself impairs calcium homeostasis. Crohn's patients have significantly elevated osteoporosis and fracture risk.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Calcium is absorbed throughout the small intestine but primarily in the duodenum and proximal jejunum (vitamin D-dependent active transport) and throughout the rest of the small intestine (passive paracellular absorption). Resection reduces absorptive surface area. Ileal resection causes bile salt malabsorption leading to fat malabsorption, which causes calcium to bind to unabsorbed fatty acids (forming calcium soaps) rather than being absorbed. This also increases oxalate absorption (kidney stone risk).
deficiency_symptoms: Numbness and tingling in fingers and toes
Chvostek sign (facial twitching when nerve tapped)
Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm with blood pressure cuff)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 13-40% have low calcium intake; osteopenia in 30-50% and osteoporosis in 15-30% of Crohn's patients

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 1000-1500 mg/day from diet and supplements combined
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 1500-2000 mg/day in divided doses; ensure adequate vitamin D for absorption

best_food_sources.notes: Usually tolerated even with mild lactose intolerance due to bacterial cultures; good protein source too
Same calcium as regular milk without lactose issues
Often higher calcium than cow's milk; shake well as calcium settles
Naturally low in lactose; aged cheeses are generally well-tolerated
Soft bones are the calcium source; also provides vitamin D and omega-3s
Check label for calcium sulfate in ingredients; soft tofu well-tolerated
Citrus may irritate; try small amounts to test tolerance
Low oxalate green vegetable; calcium is highly bioavailable (~50% absorbed vs 32% from milk)

supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Calcium citrate does not require stomach acid for absorption (critical for patients on PPIs), is better absorbed in divided doses, and causes less constipation and GI upset than calcium carbonate. It can be taken with or without food.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Calcium carbonate requires stomach acid (ineffective with PPIs), causes more constipation and bloating, and must be taken with food. Coral calcium and oyster shell calcium may contain lead.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 500-600 mg elemental calcium per dose, 2-3 times daily (body absorbs max ~500 mg at once)
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 500-600 mg calcium citrate 3 times daily (1500-1800 mg total); always co-administer with vitamin D (2000-4000 IU). Adjust based on serum calcium, 25(OH)D, and DEXA results.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Divide doses (max 500-600 mg per dose for optimal absorption). Calcium citrate can be taken without food. Ensure adequate vitamin D. Avoid taking with iron supplements (separate by 2 hours). Avoid taking with high-oxalate foods. Magnesium supports calcium metabolism—ensure adequate intake.
interactions: Iron supplements: calcium reduces iron absorption by 50-60%—separate by 2+ hours
Levothyroxine: calcium reduces absorption—separate by 4 hours
Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics: calcium chelates these—separate by 2+ hours
Bisphosphonates: calcium reduces absorption—separate by 30-60 minutes
Thiazide diuretics: reduce urinary calcium excretion, may cause hypercalcemia with supplementation
Corticosteroids: calcium supplementation essential to counteract steroid-induced bone loss
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: IV calcium gluconate for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, cardiac arrhythmia). Oral calcium is adequate for chronic supplementation in most patients; if serum calcium remains low despite high-dose oral calcium + vitamin D, evaluate for hypoparathyroidism.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum Calcium (total and ionized/corrected), 25(OH)D, PTH, DEXA scan
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Total calcium: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL; Ionized calcium: 4.5-5.3 mg/dL; Albumin-corrected calcium if albumin low
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: Total calcium <8.5 mg/dL (corrected for albumin); Ionized <4.5 mg/dL
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Every 3 months; baseline DEXA scan recommended
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months for serum calcium; DEXA every 2 years if on steroids or if osteopenia/osteoporosis present; 24-hour urine calcium annually if on high-dose supplementation
lab_monitoring.notes: Always correct calcium for albumin: Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin). Ionized calcium is more accurate. Check PTH simultaneously—elevated PTH with low/normal calcium suggests secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency. 24-hour urine calcium helps monitor for excess supplementation and kidney stone risk.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Reduce intestinal calcium absorption, increase renal calcium excretion, accelerate bone loss
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Supplement calcium 1000-1500 mg/day + vitamin D during any steroid course >3 months; consider bisphosphonate for prolonged steroid use

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Reduce calcium carbonate absorption (less effect on calcium citrate); long-term use associated with increased fracture risk
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Use calcium citrate form; ensure adequate vitamin D

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May bind calcium in the gut
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Separate dosing by 4+ hours

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: By controlling inflammation, may improve calcium absorption and bone metabolism
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Continue calcium supplementation; reassess DEXA after sustained remission

Laryngospasm (throat tightness, difficulty breathing)
Seizures
Cardiac arrhythmia (QT prolongation on EKG)
Confusion or altered mental status
Kidney stone symptoms: flank pain, blood in urine (possible excess supplementation)

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Zinc is essential for immune function, wound healing, taste perception, and intestinal epithelial integrity. Crohn's patients lose zinc through diarrhea and intestinal output, have impaired absorption from inflamed mucosa, and have increased zinc demand for tissue repair and immune function. Zinc deficiency impairs intestinal permeability and can worsen Crohn's disease activity.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Zinc is absorbed primarily in the duodenum and jejunum. Resection of these segments directly impairs absorption. Even ileal/ileocecal resection increases diarrhea and fecal output, leading to excessive zinc losses. High-output stomas or fistulae compound the problem. Post-resection patients with rapid transit have less contact time for absorption.
deficiency_symptoms: Skin rashes, especially around mouth and extremities (acrodermatitis)
Diarrhea (zinc deficiency itself causes diarrhea—vicious cycle)
Night blindness (zinc needed for vitamin A metabolism)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 25-65% of Crohn's patients; higher during active disease, diarrhea, and post-resection

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 25-40 mg/day; replace additional 12-17 mg per liter of intestinal output for high-output states

best_food_sources.notes: Best bioavailable zinc source; choose lean, tender cuts
Well-tolerated; dark meat has more zinc than white
Tender pork loin or tenderloin well-tolerated
Seeds can worsen symptoms; try pumpkin seed butter or finely ground
Good combined zinc and calcium source
Easy to digest in most preparations
Excellent source; ensure thoroughly cooked

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Zinc picolinate or zinc bisglycinate (chelated forms)
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Chelated zinc forms (picolinate, bisglycinate) have superior absorption compared to inorganic forms and cause significantly less GI upset. Zinc picolinate shows the highest bioavailability in studies.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Zinc sulfate causes nausea and GI upset in many Crohn's patients. Zinc oxide has the lowest bioavailability.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 25-50 mg elemental zinc/day for repletion; 15-25 mg/day maintenance
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 40-50 mg elemental zinc/day during repletion; add 12-17 mg per liter of intestinal output for ileostomy or high-output fistula. Maintenance 25-40 mg/day.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with protein-containing food (amino acids enhance zinc absorption). Avoid taking with high-phytate foods (whole grains, legumes) which bind zinc. Separate from iron and calcium supplements by 2 hours. Supplementing zinc long-term (>25 mg/day for >6 months) requires copper co-supplementation (2 mg copper per 25 mg zinc) to prevent copper depletion.
interactions: Iron supplements compete for absorption—separate by 2 hours
Calcium supplements reduce zinc absorption—separate by 2 hours
Penicillamine (chelator) binds zinc—separate by 2+ hours
Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics chelated by zinc—separate by 2+ hours
High-dose zinc depletes copper—always co-supplement copper
Thiazide diuretics increase urinary zinc excretion
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe malabsorption with persistent low serum zinc despite oral supplementation, short bowel syndrome with high-output stoma, or parenteral nutrition patients. IV zinc can be added to PN solutions (2.5-5 mg/day standard; 12-17 mg per liter GI fluid lost).

lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months; more frequently during active diarrhea
lab_monitoring.notes: Serum zinc is a poor marker of body stores—it drops during inflammation (negative acute phase reactant) and has diurnal variation (highest in morning fasting). Always check fasting AM sample with concurrent CRP and albumin. Alkaline phosphatase is a zinc-dependent enzyme; low ALP may suggest zinc deficiency. Hair and nail zinc can supplement but are not standardized.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor zinc levels; supplement if deficient

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Recheck zinc 3-6 months after starting biologic; adjust supplementation

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May impair zinc absorption
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Separate dosing; monitor zinc levels

Significant unexplained hair loss

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Magnesium is involved in >300 enzymatic reactions, including energy production, muscle function, nerve transmission, and bone formation. Crohn's patients lose magnesium through chronic diarrhea (the primary cause), have impaired absorption from inflamed mucosa, and may have reduced intake due to dietary restrictions. Medications like PPIs further deplete magnesium.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Magnesium is absorbed throughout the small intestine and colon. Resection of any significant bowel length reduces absorptive surface area. Ileal resection increases diarrhea and intestinal transit speed, reducing magnesium absorption time. High-output ileostomy causes dramatic magnesium losses. Colonic resection eliminates a secondary absorption site.
deficiency_symptoms: Muscle cramps and spasms (especially legs at night)
Worsening of potassium and calcium deficiency (magnesium needed for their regulation)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 20-45% of Crohn's patients; up to 80% in those with high-output stomas or extensive resection

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 600-1000 mg/day in divided doses; higher for high-output states. IV supplementation may be needed.

supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Magnesium glycinate is highly bioavailable and causes the least diarrhea of any oral form—critical for Crohn's patients already prone to diarrhea. Magnesium taurate is similarly gentle and may benefit cardiac health. Both are chelated forms with superior absorption.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Magnesium oxide (only 4% absorbed, causes osmotic diarrhea). Magnesium citrate (causes diarrhea—used as laxative). Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salts—strong laxative effect).
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 200-400 mg elemental magnesium/day in divided doses (magnesium glycinate)
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 400-600 mg elemental magnesium/day in 2-3 divided doses (glycinate form). High-output states may need 800-1000 mg/day or IV supplementation. Slow-release forms may improve tolerance.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Divide doses throughout the day (take 200 mg 2-3 times). Take with food to reduce GI effects. Vitamin B6 may enhance magnesium absorption. Avoid high-oxalate and high-phytate foods with supplement. If diarrhea worsens with any oral form, IV magnesium infusion (1-2 g MgSO4) can be used periodically.
interactions: PPIs reduce magnesium absorption significantly with long-term use (FDA black box warning for hypomagnesemia)
Loop and thiazide diuretics increase urinary magnesium excretion
Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics chelated by magnesium—separate by 2+ hours
Bisphosphonates: magnesium reduces absorption—separate by 2+ hours
Aminoglycosides increase renal magnesium wasting
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) increase renal magnesium wasting
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Persistent hypomagnesemia despite high-dose oral supplementation, high-output stoma or fistula, short bowel syndrome, severe diarrhea, or symptomatic hypomagnesemia (arrhythmia, seizures). IV magnesium sulfate 1-2 g over 1 hour, repeated as needed. Some patients need weekly IV magnesium infusions.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum Magnesium; RBC Magnesium for better tissue estimate; 24-hour urine magnesium for renal wasting
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Serum: 1.7-2.2 mg/dL (0.70-0.91 mmol/L); RBC Magnesium: 4.2-6.8 mg/dL
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: Serum <1.2 mg/dL (<0.49 mmol/L) — risk of cardiac arrhythmia
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6 months; more frequently with high-output stoma or diuretic use
lab_monitoring.notes: Serum magnesium is a poor indicator of total body magnesium (only 1% of body magnesium is in blood). Can be normal despite significant tissue depletion. RBC magnesium is more reflective of intracellular stores. 24-hour urine magnesium <24 mg/day with low serum magnesium suggests GI loss rather than renal wasting. Always check concurrent potassium and calcium—hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia and hypocalcemia refractory to treatment.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor magnesium every 6 months on long-term PPIs; supplement proactively

interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor and supplement during steroid courses

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: By reducing stool output, helps retain magnesium
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: May use adjunctively to reduce magnesium losses in high-output states

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis, cell division, and red blood cell production. Crohn's patients are at risk due to proximal small bowel inflammation (where folate is absorbed), reduced dietary intake of green vegetables during flares, and medication effects—sulfasalazine directly inhibits folate absorption and methotrexate is a folate antagonist. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and elevates homocysteine (cardiovascular risk).
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Folate is absorbed primarily in the proximal jejunum. While this segment is less commonly resected, any reduction in small bowel length reduces folate absorption capacity. Rapid transit post-resection shortens contact time. Jejunal resection directly impairs folate absorption. Bacterial overgrowth (common post-resection) can consume dietary folate.
deficiency_symptoms: Diarrhea (folate deficiency itself causes malabsorption—vicious cycle)
Neural tube defects in pregnancy (critical for women of childbearing age)
Poor growth of mucosal lining (impairs gut healing)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 20-40% of Crohn's patients; up to 54% in those on sulfasalazine

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 800-1000 mcg/day; 1 mg/day mandatory if on sulfasalazine or methotrexate
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 1000-2000 mcg/day; higher if on folate-depleting medications

supplement_guidance.why_this_form: L-methylfolate does not require enzymatic conversion by MTHFR (up to 40% of population has reduced MTHFR activity). It is directly usable, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and does not mask B12 deficiency the way high-dose folic acid can (though this is debated). It bypasses any absorption-conversion bottleneck.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: High-dose folic acid (>1 mg) without checking B12 first—can mask B12 deficiency and allow neurological damage to progress. Unmetabolized folic acid from synthetic supplementation may have health concerns at high doses.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 1 mg L-methylfolate/day or 1 mg folic acid/day
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 1-5 mg L-methylfolate/day depending on degree of malabsorption and medication use. Always co-monitor B12.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Can be taken with or without food. If on methotrexate, take folate on non-methotrexate days (some protocols use leucovorin/folinic acid instead). Always ensure B12 is adequate before starting high-dose folate supplementation.
interactions: Sulfasalazine competitively inhibits folate absorption—always co-supplement
Methotrexate is a direct folate antagonist—folate or folinic acid supplementation is standard of care
Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate increase folate metabolism and reduce levels
Trimethoprim (antibiotic) is a weak folate antagonist
Cholestyramine may reduce folate absorption
High-dose folic acid may mask B12 deficiency—always check B12
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe jejunal disease or resection with documented malabsorption despite oral supplementation. IV or IM folinic acid (leucovorin) 5-15 mg can be used. Parenteral folate is available for PN patients.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum Folate and RBC Folate (RBC folate reflects longer-term status); also Homocysteine
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Serum folate: >3 ng/mL (>7 nmol/L); RBC folate: >140 ng/mL (>317 nmol/L)
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: Serum folate <3 ng/mL; RBC folate <140 ng/mL
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: Serum folate <2 ng/mL; megaloblastic changes on blood smear
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months; more frequently if on sulfasalazine or methotrexate
lab_monitoring.notes: RBC folate is more reliable than serum folate (which reflects recent intake). Elevated homocysteine (>15 umol/L) with normal/low folate suggests functional deficiency. Always check B12 simultaneously—macrocytic anemia can be from either or both. MCV >100 fL on CBC should prompt B12 and folate check.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Both require adequate folate for DNA synthesis; deficiency may increase bone marrow suppression risk

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May reduce folate absorption slightly
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor folate levels during prolonged steroid courses

Pregnancy with low folate levels (neural tube defect risk)

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Selenium is a critical antioxidant (as selenoproteins including glutathione peroxidase) and supports thyroid function and immune regulation. Crohn's patients have increased oxidative stress consuming selenium stores, malabsorption from inflamed mucosa, and dietary restrictions limiting intake. Low selenium is associated with more severe IBD outcomes.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Selenium is absorbed primarily in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Resection of any small bowel length reduces absorptive capacity. Increased diarrhea and intestinal output post-resection lead to excess selenium losses. Short bowel syndrome patients are at highest risk.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Potassium is critical for muscle contraction, nerve function, fluid balance, and cardiac rhythm. Crohn's patients lose potassium through chronic diarrhea (the major cause), vomiting, fistula output, and medication effects (corticosteroids increase renal potassium excretion). Hypokalemia can be dangerous and is common during flares.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Potassium is absorbed throughout the GI tract, with significant absorption in the small intestine and colon. Resection reduces absorptive surface and often increases diarrhea. Ileostomy output is high in potassium—patients with high-output ileostomy are at particular risk. Colonic resection eliminates a major potassium absorption site.
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 6-20% have clinically significant hypokalemia; subclinical depletion likely much higher, especially during flares

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 4000-5000+ mg/day; guided by serum levels and output volume. IV replacement for severe depletion.

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Potassium chloride (KCl) extended-release tablets or oral solution for acute repletion; potassium gluconate or citrate for maintenance
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Potassium chloride is the standard for repletion as it addresses concurrent chloride losses from diarrhea. Extended-release forms reduce GI irritation. Potassium citrate may benefit patients with metabolic acidosis (common post-resection).
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Immediate-release potassium tablets can cause GI ulceration—always use wax-matrix extended-release or liquid form. Avoid high-dose potassium in patients with renal impairment.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 20-40 mEq/day (750-1500 mg elemental potassium) for mild depletion; divided doses
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 40-80 mEq/day (1500-3000 mg) in divided doses for moderate depletion. Severe: IV potassium 10-20 mEq/hour (max 40 mEq/hour in monitored setting). Replace magnesium first if both are low (hypokalemia is refractory to treatment without adequate magnesium).
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with food and a full glass of water to reduce GI irritation. Extended-release tablets should not be crushed. Liquid forms are fastest absorbed. Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) provide potassium in balanced electrolyte form. Replace magnesium simultaneously if both are depleted.
interactions: ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce potassium excretion—risk of hyperkalemia with supplementation
Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride) reduce potassium excretion—risk of hyperkalemia
Loop diuretics (furosemide) and thiazides increase potassium loss—may need increased supplementation
Corticosteroids increase potassium loss
NSAIDs can increase potassium retention—monitor
Digoxin: hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Serum potassium <2.5 mEq/L, symptomatic hypokalemia (arrhythmia, severe weakness), inability to take oral, or refractory hypokalemia. IV potassium chloride via central line (max 40 mEq/hour with cardiac monitoring). Always correct hypomagnesemia simultaneously.

lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 3-6 months; with every BMP. Increase frequency during flares, steroid use, or diuretic therapy

EKG changes: flattened T waves, U waves, ST depression (hypokalemia). Always check magnesium with potassium—hypokalemia may be refractory until hypomagnesemia is corrected.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Unlike the general population where sodium excess is the concern, Crohn's patients—especially those with ileostomy or significant diarrhea—are at risk of sodium depletion. Sodium is lost in large quantities through diarrhea and intestinal output. Hyponatremia causes dehydration, hypotension, and can be life-threatening. Post-resection patients must often deliberately increase sodium intake.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: The colon is the major site of sodium and water reabsorption. Ileocecal or colonic resection eliminates this absorptive capacity, resulting in sodium-rich ileostomy output (typically 80-130 mEq/L sodium). High-output ileostomy can lose 1-2 liters/day, representing massive sodium losses. Even with intact colon, ileal resection increases diarrhea and sodium losses.
deficiency_symptoms: Dehydration (despite adequate fluid intake if sodium is not replaced)
Dizziness and lightheadedness when standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Concentrated dark urine and reduced urine output
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 10-30% of Crohn's patients during flares; up to 50-80% in those with high-output ileostomy if not properly managed

recommended_daily_intake.general_adult: <2300 mg/day (general public guideline to limit intake)
recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: Individualized; may need 3000-5000 mg/day during active diarrhea
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: Ileostomy patients may need 4000-8000 mg/day or more to match output losses. Guided by urine sodium (should be >20 mEq/L).

Warm, soothing, and well-tolerated. Excellent for flares. Provides sodium and some other electrolytes.

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Oral rehydration solution (glucose-sodium co-transport solution) or sodium chloride tablets/capsules
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: ORS uses glucose-sodium co-transport (SGLT1) to maximize sodium absorption even with reduced bowel length. This mechanism remains functional in the remaining small bowel. Salt tablets provide concentrated sodium when ORS volume is not tolerated.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Hypotonic fluids (plain water, Gatorade, tea, juice) can actually worsen ileostomy output and sodium depletion by osmotic effect. Diet should include sodium, not just free water.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: Individualized based on output: 1-2 liters of ORS/day for high-output ileostomy; sodium chloride tablets 1-2 g 2-4 times daily
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: Match losses: measure ileostomy output and replace sodium proportionally. Typical ileostomy sodium concentration is 90-120 mEq/L. For 1L output, replace approximately 2-3 g sodium. ORS is the most efficient vehicle.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Sip ORS throughout the day rather than large boluses. Glucose is essential for sodium co-transport—plain salt water is much less effective. St. Mark's solution (homemade ORS: 6 tsp sugar + 1 tsp salt per liter water) is a cost-effective option. Restrict hypotonic fluids to 500 mL/day if ileostomy output is high. Loperamide before meals can reduce output.
interactions: Loperamide: helps reduce sodium and fluid losses from ileostomy—often co-prescribed
Codeine phosphate: reduces intestinal secretion and transit, helping sodium retention
ACE inhibitors/ARBs: may worsen hypotension in sodium-depleted patients
Diuretics: exacerbate sodium and fluid losses—use with extreme caution post-resection
PPIs: may reduce gastric sodium absorption
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe dehydration with hyponatremia <125 mEq/L, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability. IV normal saline (0.9% NaCl) or Ringer's lactate for acute repletion. Some high-output ileostomy patients require scheduled IV saline infusions (e.g., 1L IV NS 2-3 times per week at home).

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum Sodium (part of BMP); Urine Sodium (spot or 24-hour); Stool/Ostomy output volume
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Serum sodium: 136-145 mEq/L; Urine sodium: >20 mEq/L indicates adequate sodium status
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: Serum sodium <136 mEq/L (hyponatremia); Urine sodium <20 mEq/L (body is sodium-avid, indicating depletion)
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: Serum sodium <125 mEq/L (severe hyponatremia—seizure and brain edema risk)
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Weekly for first month post-ileostomy creation, then every 2-4 weeks until stable, then every 3 months
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 3-6 months; more frequently during illness, flares, hot weather, or medication changes. Teach patients to monitor urine color and output volume.
lab_monitoring.notes: Urine sodium is a better indicator of sodium balance than serum sodium (serum is tightly regulated until depletion is severe). Urine sodium <20 mEq/L = the kidneys are desperately conserving sodium, indicating total body depletion even if serum sodium is still normal. Track ileostomy output volume daily—>1.5L/day warrants action.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) have potent anti-inflammatory properties through production of resolvins and protectins, suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6), and modulation of NF-kB signaling. Crohn's patients typically have an unfavorable omega-6 to omega-3 ratio due to Western diet patterns. While not a traditional 'deficiency' nutrient, omega-3 status affects inflammatory tone and may influence disease activity.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Long-chain fatty acid absorption requires bile salts, pancreatic lipase, and intact small bowel mucosa. Ileal resection disrupts bile salt recycling, causing fat malabsorption that affects all long-chain fatty acids including EPA/DHA. Patients may also avoid fatty fish and oily foods due to steatorrhea, further reducing intake.
deficiency_symptoms: Hair that is dry, brittle, or falling out
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: Suboptimal omega-3 levels found in 50-70% of Crohn's patients based on omega-3 index testing; overtly deficient in 20-30%

recommended_daily_intake.general_adult: 250-500 mg combined EPA + DHA/day (no official RDA; Adequate Intake for ALA is 1.1-1.6 g/day)
recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 1000-2000 mg combined EPA + DHA/day for anti-inflammatory benefit
recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 2000-3000 mg EPA + DHA/day; triglyceride form for better absorption in fat malabsorption; consider enteric-coated

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Triglyceride (TG) form fish oil or re-esterified triglyceride (rTG); alternatively, algal oil (vegan DHA+EPA)
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Triglyceride form has 70% better absorption than ethyl ester (EE) form. This is critical in fat malabsorption states. Re-esterified TG combines high concentration with TG bioavailability. Algal oil provides DHA+EPA without fish, useful for those who cannot tolerate fish oil.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Ethyl ester form (most cheap fish oils) has poor absorption, especially in patients with impaired bile salt function. Cod liver oil in high doses may provide excessive vitamin A.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 1000-2000 mg EPA+DHA per day (not total fish oil—check label for actual EPA+DHA content)
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 2000-3000 mg EPA+DHA/day in triglyceride form; consider emulsified liquid fish oil for better absorption. Split into 2-3 doses with meals. Enteric-coated may reduce fishy reflux.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Always take with a fat-containing meal. Emulsified (liquid) fish oil absorbs 3x better than capsules in malabsorption. MCT oil can be combined to improve absorption. Store fish oil in refrigerator to reduce oxidation and fishy taste. Enteric-coated capsules reduce reflux but may delay absorption.
interactions: Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs): omega-3 >3 g/day may increase bleeding risk—monitor INR
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel): additive bleeding risk at high omega-3 doses
Orlistat reduces omega-3 absorption
Immunosuppressants: theoretical enhanced immune modulation—clinical significance unclear
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe fat malabsorption with steatorrhea despite triglyceride-form and emulsified supplements. IV lipid emulsions containing omega-3 (Omegaven, SMOFlipid) can be used in parenteral nutrition patients.

lab_monitoring.normal_range: Omega-3 Index: 8-12% (optimal zone for anti-inflammatory benefit)
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Baseline and at 6 months to assess supplementation response
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Annually if supplementing; more of a lifestyle optimization marker than critical lab
lab_monitoring.notes: Omega-3 Index is the most validated marker, measured as a dried blood spot test (finger prick kits available). Not routinely covered by insurance. The goal of 8-12% is based on cardiovascular and anti-inflammatory data. Most Western populations average 4-5%. IBD patients may benefit from higher targets.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis (wound healing), immune function, and is a powerful antioxidant. It also enhances non-heme iron absorption—critical for iron-deficient Crohn's patients. Crohn's patients are at risk due to reduced fruit/vegetable intake during flares, increased oxidative stress consuming vitamin C reserves, and malabsorption from inflamed mucosa.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Vitamin C is absorbed primarily in the distal small intestine (ileum and jejunum). Resection of these segments reduces absorption. Post-surgical healing demands increased vitamin C for collagen synthesis. High-output states lead to excessive losses. Rapid transit reduces absorption time.
deficiency_symptoms: Scurvy (severe): loose teeth, hemorrhage, bone pain
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 15-30% of Crohn's patients have suboptimal levels; overt deficiency less common (~5%) but underdiagnosed

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 500-1000 mg/day in divided doses; higher during wound healing period

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Buffered vitamin C (calcium ascorbate or sodium ascorbate) or liposomal vitamin C
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Buffered forms are less acidic and gentler on the GI tract—important for Crohn's patients with sensitive mucosa. Liposomal vitamin C has enhanced absorption and bypasses some intestinal transport limitations.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Pure ascorbic acid in high doses (>500 mg) can cause diarrhea and stomach upset. Chewable vitamin C tablets can erode tooth enamel. Avoid >2000 mg/day (increases oxalate kidney stone risk, especially problematic post-ileal resection).
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 250-500 mg buffered vitamin C 1-2 times daily
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 500 mg buffered vitamin C 2 times daily (1000 mg total); higher during wound healing (up to 2000 mg/day for 4-6 weeks post-surgery). Reduce to 500 mg/day maintenance. Monitor urinary oxalate if ileal resection (increased kidney stone risk).
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Split doses (absorption efficiency decreases above ~200 mg per dose). Take with iron supplements to enhance iron absorption by 2-3 fold. Avoid high-dose vitamin C >2000 mg/day long-term due to oxalate kidney stone risk (especially after ileal resection where oxalate absorption increases). Vitamin C is water-soluble—excess is excreted renally.

High-dose vitamin C may increase aluminum absorption from antacids
May reduce vitamin B12 levels if taken simultaneously—separate by 2 hours
High-dose vitamin C may interfere with certain lab tests (glucose, occult blood)
Increases oxalate excretion—risk of calcium oxalate kidney stones, especially post-ileal resection
May reduce effectiveness of some chemotherapy drugs
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe malabsorption or short bowel syndrome. IV vitamin C (ascorbic acid injection) can be used: 200-500 mg IV daily during acute deficiency or post-surgical healing. Parenteral nutrition should include vitamin C (200 mg/day standard PN multivitamin).

Levels drop rapidly during acute illness/inflammation (consumed as antioxidant). Leukocyte (buffy coat) vitamin C is a better marker of tissue stores but is labor-intensive and rarely available.

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Copper is essential for iron metabolism (ceruloplasmin), connective tissue formation, immune function, and neurological health. Crohn's patients are at risk from malabsorption, and critically, from zinc supplementation (which is common in Crohn's management)—zinc and copper compete for absorption via the same transporter (DMT-1). Copper deficiency can mimic B12 deficiency neurologically.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Copper is absorbed primarily in the stomach and duodenum. While these segments are rarely resected in Crohn's, increased intestinal transit, diarrhea, and high-output states increase copper losses. The main post-resection risk is iatrogenic copper depletion from zinc supplementation prescribed to replace zinc losses.
deficiency_symptoms: Anemia (microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic) unresponsive to iron supplementation
Neutropenia (low white blood cells—increased infection risk)
Skin depigmentation and premature graying of hair
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 5-15% overall; significantly higher (up to 30%) in those taking zinc supplements without copper co-supplementation

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 2-3 mg/day if on zinc supplementation; monitor levels

supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Copper sulfate can cause GI upset. Avoid copper supplementation without established need—copper excess is hepatotoxic (Wilson disease-like presentation).
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 2 mg/day when supplementing zinc >25 mg/day (standard ratio: 1 mg copper per 15 mg zinc)
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 2-3 mg/day if on zinc supplementation; monitor serum copper and ceruloplasmin every 6 months. Adjust based on levels.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Separate from zinc supplements by at least 2 hours (they compete for the same transporter). Take with food to reduce GI upset. Vitamin C in moderate doses may enhance copper absorption, but high-dose vitamin C (>1500 mg) may reduce copper absorption. Avoid taking with antacids.
interactions: Zinc supplements competitively inhibit copper absorption (most important interaction)
High-dose vitamin C (>1500 mg) may reduce copper absorption
Antacids reduce copper absorption
Penicillamine chelates copper (used in Wilson disease—contraindicated in copper deficiency)
Iron supplements may compete for absorption at high doses
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe malabsorption or short bowel syndrome. IV copper (copper chloride) can be added to parenteral nutrition (0.3-0.5 mg/day standard; up to 1.5 mg/day for repletion).

lab_monitoring.normal_range: Serum copper: 70-140 mcg/dL (11-22 umol/L); Ceruloplasmin: 20-35 mg/dL
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: Serum copper <50 mcg/dL with hematologic or neurologic manifestations
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Baseline, then every 6 months if on zinc supplementation
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months if on zinc supplements; annually otherwise
lab_monitoring.notes: Ceruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant—can be elevated during inflammation, masking copper depletion. Check concurrent CRP. Free (non-ceruloplasmin-bound) copper can be calculated but is complex. 24-hour urine copper helps assess total body status. If unexplained anemia or neutropenia develops while on zinc, check copper immediately.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Most important interaction: zinc induces intestinal metallothionein which binds copper and prevents its absorption
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: ALWAYS co-supplement copper when zinc >25 mg/day. Ratio of 1 mg copper per 15 mg zinc. Separate doses by 2 hours.

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May reduce copper absorption by raising gastric pH
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor copper levels in long-term PPI users

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Copper deficiency can cause pancytopenia mimicking drug-induced bone marrow suppression
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Check copper before attributing cytopenias solely to medication

warning_signs_need_immediate_attention: Unexplained anemia unresponsive to iron supplementation
Neutropenia (ANC <1500) while on zinc supplements—check copper immediately
Neurological symptoms (neuropathy, myelopathy) mimicking B12 deficiency but with normal B12
Pancytopenia of unclear cause

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Chromium enhances insulin signaling and is involved in glucose and lipid metabolism. While overt deficiency is rare, Crohn's patients with malabsorption, extensive bowel disease, or on parenteral nutrition may develop deficiency. Chromium deficiency can cause glucose intolerance and insulin resistance, relevant because corticosteroid-treated Crohn's patients already face glucose dysregulation.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Chromium is absorbed throughout the small intestine, primarily in the jejunum. Resection reduces absorptive surface area. Increased intestinal transit and diarrhea increase losses. Patients on parenteral nutrition without adequate chromium supplementation are at highest risk.
deficiency_symptoms: Glucose intolerance and elevated blood sugar
Peripheral neuropathy (rare, mainly in PN patients)
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: Unknown; rarely measured. Likely 5-10% clinically significant deficiency; subclinical depletion may be more common in extensive disease or PN patients

recommended_daily_intake.post_resection: 50-100 mcg/day; higher if glucose intolerance develops or if on PN without chromium

supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Chromium picolinate is the most studied form with the best bioavailability. Picolinic acid chelation enhances intestinal absorption.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Chromium chloride has very low absorption (<2%). Avoid chromium nicotinate in high doses.
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 200-500 mcg/day if deficient or glucose intolerant. For PN patients, 10-15 mcg/day IV.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Vitamin C may enhance chromium absorption. Antacids and PPIs may reduce absorption. High iron intake may compete with chromium absorption. Phytates reduce absorption.
interactions: Insulin and oral hypoglycemics: chromium may enhance their effects—monitor blood glucose
Corticosteroids: compound glucose intolerance; chromium supplementation may partially offset steroid-induced hyperglycemia
NSAIDs may increase chromium absorption
Antacids reduce chromium absorption
Iron supplements may compete for absorption
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: PN patients require IV chromium (chromic chloride) 10-15 mcg/day added to PN solution. Rarely needed outside PN context.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum/Plasma Chromium (not widely standardized); Glucose and HbA1c as functional markers
lab_monitoring.normal_range: Serum chromium: 0.05-0.50 mcg/L (variable by lab); no well-established reference range
lab_monitoring.deficient_threshold: No well-established threshold; functional deficiency suggested by unexplained glucose intolerance in at-risk patients
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: Not established; clinical diagnosis based on glucose intolerance responding to chromium supplementation
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Not routinely tested; check if unexplained glucose intolerance develops
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Monitor glucose/HbA1c; test chromium only if clinical suspicion of deficiency
lab_monitoring.notes: Serum chromium is a poor marker of body stores and is not well-standardized across laboratories. The most practical approach is to monitor fasting glucose and HbA1c, and consider a trial of chromium supplementation if unexplained glucose intolerance develops in a malnourished Crohn's patient. Contamination in blood draws is common (stainless steel needles contain chromium).

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Steroids cause hyperglycemia; chromium deficiency exacerbates this
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Consider chromium supplementation (200 mcg/day) during prolonged steroid courses, especially if glucose rises

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May reduce chromium absorption
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Separate dosing if supplementing chromium

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Chromium may enhance metformin effect on glucose
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor blood glucose more frequently if combining

warning_signs_need_immediate_attention: New-onset hyperglycemia in a malnourished Crohn's patient (consider chromium deficiency alongside steroid-induced diabetes)
Peripheral neuropathy of unclear cause in a PN patient (check chromium among other micronutrients)
Occupational chromium exposure toxicity signs: kidney damage, lung irritation (different from supplementation)

nutrients.why_crohns_patients_need_monitoring: Phosphorus is critical for bone mineralization, energy metabolism (ATP), acid-base balance, and cell signaling. Crohn's patients are at risk from malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency (which impairs phosphorus absorption), chronic use of aluminum-containing antacids (which bind phosphorus), and refeeding syndrome risk when resuming nutrition after prolonged fasting or severe malnutrition.
nutrients.why_resection_makes_it_worse: Phosphorus is absorbed throughout the small intestine, with the most active absorption in the duodenum and jejunum (vitamin D-dependent). Resection reduces absorptive surface area. Vitamin D deficiency from ileal resection compounds the problem by reducing active phosphorus absorption. Refeeding syndrome risk is highest in post-surgical patients who have been NPO (nothing by mouth) or severely malnourished.
nutrients.deficiency_prevalence_in_crohns: 5-15% have low serum phosphorus; refeeding hypophosphatemia risk in 15-30% of malnourished IBD patients requiring nutritional support

recommended_daily_intake.crohns_patient: 700-1200 mg/day depending on absorption and medication use

supplement_guidance.preferred_form: Sodium phosphate or potassium phosphate (Neutra-Phos) for oral repletion
supplement_guidance.why_this_form: Inorganic phosphate salts provide highly bioavailable phosphorus. Combination sodium-potassium phosphate (Neutra-Phos) provides phosphorus without excessive sodium or potassium load. Phosphorus is well-absorbed orally in most situations.
supplement_guidance.forms_to_avoid: Avoid phosphorus-containing enemas or bowel preps (risk of severe hyperphosphatemia). Calcium phosphate is poorly absorbed.
supplement_guidance.typical_dose: 500-1000 mg elemental phosphorus/day in divided doses for mild deficiency
supplement_guidance.post_resection_dose: 1000-1500 mg/day in divided doses for moderate deficiency. Severe or refeeding hypophosphatemia: IV potassium phosphate or sodium phosphate (0.08-0.64 mmol/kg over 6-12 hours depending on severity). Critical to monitor during refeeding.
supplement_guidance.absorption_tips: Take with meals for best tolerance. Vitamin D enhances phosphorus absorption. Avoid taking with aluminum-containing antacids (they bind phosphorus). Calcium supplements can bind phosphorus—separate by 2 hours if using high doses of both. Phosphorus absorption is reduced by phytates.
interactions: Aluminum-containing antacids bind phosphorus in the gut—major cause of depletion in Crohn's patients using antacids
Calcium supplements can reduce phosphorus absorption at high doses
Sucralfate contains aluminum—reduces phosphorus absorption
Vitamin D enhances phosphorus absorption (beneficial interaction)
Insulin drives phosphorus into cells—relevant in refeeding syndrome
Corticosteroids may affect phosphorus metabolism
supplement_guidance.when_oral_wont_work: Severe hypophosphatemia (<1.5 mg/dL), symptomatic hypophosphatemia (weakness, respiratory compromise, confusion), refeeding syndrome, or inability to tolerate oral intake. IV phosphate (potassium phosphate or sodium phosphate) with cardiac monitoring. Replace over 6-12 hours to avoid rapid shifts.

lab_monitoring.test_name: Serum Phosphorus (Phosphate); also check calcium, magnesium, vitamin D, and PTH
lab_monitoring.severely_deficient_threshold: <1.5 mg/dL (<0.48 mmol/L) — risk of respiratory failure and rhabdomyolysis
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_first_year_post_surger: Every 3 months; DAILY during nutritional repletion in malnourished patients (refeeding protocol)
lab_monitoring.testing_frequency_ongoing: Every 6-12 months; more frequently during nutritional rehabilitation or flares
lab_monitoring.notes: Phosphorus shifts into cells with insulin release (after eating carbohydrates) and can drop dramatically during refeeding in malnourished patients. ALWAYS check phosphorus before initiating TPN or aggressive enteral feeding in malnourished Crohn's patients. Refeeding protocol: start feeds at 10-15 kcal/kg/day, supplement thiamine and phosphorus prophylactically, and advance slowly. Serum phosphorus is a poor indicator of total body phosphorus (most is in bone).

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Bind dietary and supplemental phosphorus, causing significant depletion with chronic use
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Avoid aluminum-containing antacids in Crohn's patients; use calcium carbonate or PPIs instead

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: May increase urinary phosphorus excretion; also increase catabolism
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Monitor phosphorus during prolonged steroid courses

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Contains aluminum; binds phosphorus
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Avoid long-term use; monitor phosphorus if used

interactions_with_crohns_medications.effect: Refeeding syndrome risk with phosphorus depletion; inadequate phosphorus in PN solution
interactions_with_crohns_medications.recommendation: Check phosphorus daily when initiating PN; supplement 20-40 mmol/day in PN; increase for refeeding

warning_signs_need_immediate_attention: Serum phosphorus <1.5 mg/dL (severe hypophosphatemia)
Respiratory muscle weakness or difficulty breathing during refeeding
Confusion or altered mental status in a malnourished patient receiving nutrition
Rhabdomyolysis: muscle pain, weakness, dark urine (myoglobinuria)
Heart failure symptoms during refeeding: rapid heartbeat, fluid retention, shortness of breath
Any rapid decline in phosphorus after starting enteral or parenteral nutrition
